acceptedAnswer.text: Dental bonding is generally a comfortable procedure. In most cases, it does not require local anaesthetic because little or no natural tooth structure needs to be removed. The dentist applies the composite resin directly to the tooth surface, building up shape and contour in layers. Some patients experience mild sensitivity during the conditioning step, but this is typically brief. If you have concerns about discomfort, discuss this with your dentist beforehand so they can ensure you feel at ease throughout the appointment.

mainEntity.name: How long does composite bonding last on front teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: The longevity of composite bonding varies depending on several factors, including the location of the bonding, the patient's oral habits, and how well the bonding is maintained. In general, composite bonding on front teeth may last between five and ten years before repair or replacement is needed. Regular dental check-ups, good oral hygiene, and avoiding habits such as nail-biting or chewing hard objects can help extend the lifespan of the bonding. Your dentist can provide a more personalised estimate during your consultation.

mainEntity.name: Can bonding make my teeth look more natural?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, when carried out by a skilled dentist, composite bonding can significantly improve the natural appearance of teeth. The dentist selects composite shades that closely match your existing teeth and can recreate subtle features such as surface texture, translucency, and gentle contours. The goal is typically to enhance your smile in a way that looks authentic rather than artificial. Results depend on the individual case and the expertise of the treating dentist, so it is important to discuss your expectations during a consultation.

Composite resin can gradually develop surface staining, particularly with regular exposure to tea, coffee, red wine, or tobacco. However, surface stains can often be reduced or removed with professional polishing during routine dental hygiene appointments. Choosing high-quality composite materials and maintaining good oral hygiene habits can help minimise staining. Your dentist can advise on the best way to care for bonded teeth and keep them looking their best for as long as possible.

Bonding is a versatile treatment, but it is not suitable for every situation. Patients with significant tooth decay, gum disease, or severe structural damage may need alternative treatments before or instead of bonding. Similarly, those with very heavy bite forces or untreated bruxism may find that bonding wears more quickly. A thorough clinical examination is necessary to determine whether bonding is the most appropriate option for your specific needs and goals.

mainEntity.name: How is bonding different from veneers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding involves applying resin material directly to the tooth and sculpting it into shape during a single appointment. Porcelain veneers are custom-made in a laboratory and require a small amount of enamel to be removed before they are bonded in place. Veneers tend to be more resistant to staining and may last longer, but they involve a more permanent alteration to the natural tooth. Both options have their advantages, and the best choice depends on your individual clinical situation and aesthetic goals.
